finding.claim: Lenient base64url decoding lets an attacker produce many distinct compact-JWS strings for one valid signature (non-canonical trailing bits and ignored non-alphabet characters in the signature segment). Any application that uses the raw token string as a unique key (denylist, replay cache, single-use tokens) can be bypassed. Claims and signature are unchanged, so this is not forgery.
finding.source: Attacker holds one valid signed token (e.g., a logged-out or replayed token) and edits only the last character of the signature segment, or inserts an ignored character, in the compact serialization sent to the app.
finding.sink: jwt/api_jws.py:362 base64url_decode(crypto_segment) accepts the altered string; api_jws.py:416 alg_obj.verify() still succeeds, so jwt.decode returns the claims.

trace.note: jwt.rsplit(b'.',1) splits off the raw signature segment; the signing input is the original header.payload bytes, so only the signature segment varies
crypto_segment goes to base64url_decode with no canonical-form check
padding is computed from the raw length; no rejection of trailing non-zero unused bits
base64.urlsafe_b64decode is called with validate=False, so non-alphabet characters are silently discarded
HMAC uses hmac.compare_digest on the decoded bytes, so the altered string verifies

finding.guards_checked: Signature covers raw header.payload bytes, so header and payload cannot be altered. HMAC uses compare_digest. EC length check at utils.py:87 bounds length only, not canonical bits. No code in the repo checks token-string uniqueness; any denylist is the application's responsibility. Not executed (Bash disabled); verified by reading only. Impact depends on the consuming app relying on token-string identity, so severity is low.
